terms.grammar: conjunction: joins words or clauses of equal weight
evidence: Cic. Att. 12.9.1: nec erat quod scrīberem, et somnus urgēbat
terms.comment: The plain “and”. Repeated, et … et is “both … and”. In narration it should not be the only joint between clauses: Latin ties actions together with a participle, an ablative absolute, a cum-clause or a relative, or sets them side by side with no word at all, as Caesar does (Hostēs terga vertunt; fugientibus equitēs occurrunt, B.G. 7.88). A single et between clauses with different subjects is classical (Cic. Att. 4.2.4); what sounds translated is et as the joint of every sentence. For “and not” Latin says nec.

terms.grammar: enclitic conjunction, added to the first word of the second member
evidence: Cato Agr. praef. 2: bonum agricolam bonumque colōnum
terms.comment: Joins two things that belong together, or adds the last member of a pair: diēs noctēsque, day and night; terrā marīque, by land and sea (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: conjunction: atque before vowels and consonants, ac only before consonants
evidence: Cic. Att. 16.6.4: dēliciīs atque amōribus meīs
terms.comment: Joins closely, with weight on what is added; often two near-synonyms (Lewis & Short: “a close internal connection”, where et joins different things). Etiam atque etiam, again and again.

phrases.latin: nec erat quod scrīberem, et somnus urgēbat
phrases.english: there was nothing to write, and sleep was pressing

phrases.latin: virum bonum quom laudābant, ita laudābant: bonum agricolam bonumque colōnum
phrases.english: when they praised a good man, they praised him like this: a good farmer and a good husbandman

phrases.latin: nam mihi ante oculōs diēs noctēsque versāris
phrases.english: for you are before my eyes day and night

phrases.latin: Cicerō bellissimus tibi salūtem plūrimam dīcit. etiam atque etiam valē.
phrases.english: our lovely Cicero sends you his warmest love. Goodbye, again and again.

phrases.latin: Hostēs terga vertunt; fugientibus equitēs occurrunt.
phrases.english: The enemy turn and run; the cavalry meet them as they flee. (Two clauses with no “and”.)
